app.description: Official data for every economy: how many grams of gold an hour or a month of work is worth, and what that gold buys locally.
app.footer: The dataset is re-fetched from the official sources and re-checked by GitHub Actions (daily, and whenever the pipeline code changes); every number can be traced to its source file and checksum under “Methods & sources”.
app.lede: Wages in every economy are first converted into grams of gold; then we look at what those grams buy locally. The figures come from official publishers — the World Bank, the International Labour Organization (ILOSTAT) and the OECD, and, for the economies listed under Methods, the survey publishers whose own releases continue ILOSTAT’s series for years ILOSTAT has not yet republished — and every source file is archived, traceable and recomputable.
app.stale#one: {n:int} source file was not updated in this run; its previous snapshot is used
app.stale#other: {n:int} source files were not updated in this run; their previous snapshots are used
app.title: How much gold is an hour of work worth — and what does that gold buy?
buys.aria: What a gram of gold buys, by economy
buys.col_diet: 1 g of gold = days of healthy diet
buys.note_consumption: International dollars = US-dollar price of 1 g of gold ÷ the economy’s price level of household consumption (purchasing power parity ÷ market exchange rate, World Bank WDI). It covers all household consumption, including housing and services. The international dollar is the unit of the International Comparison Program: it has the purchasing power of a US dollar in the United States.
buys.note_diet: Healthy diet: the World Bank Food Prices for Nutrition cost of the cheapest healthy diet for one person for one day (local currency, current prices). It covers food only, and takes the cheapest available foods in each food group — not a typical household’s shopping basket. Per the World Bank’s description of the database, the foods are priced in the International Comparison Program’s benchmark year, and the cost in other years is estimated from it with consumer price indices.
buys.sub: Local gold prices are the US-dollar price × the exchange rate, so in dollars a gram is worth the same everywhere; but converted into local currency, the same gram buys more where prices are lower. The differences in this step are the differences in price levels.

gold.note_concepts#one: Concepts can differ a lot: where an economy has both for the same year, an ILOSTAT survey’s average monthly wage is {min:d2}–{max:d2} times OECD’s full-time-equivalent average wage (median {median:d2}; lower in {below:pct0} of the {n:int} pair in this dataset), so rankings across different concepts should be read with care; each economy’s profile shows the figures used for it.
gold.note_concepts#other: Concepts can differ a lot: where an economy has both for the same year, an ILOSTAT survey’s average monthly wage is {min:d2}–{max:d2} times OECD’s full-time-equivalent average wage (median {median:d2}; lower in {below:pct0} of the {n:int} pairs in this dataset), so rankings across different concepts should be read with care; each economy’s profile shows the figures used for it.
gold.note_fx: The official rate is checked each year against the factor the World Bank used to convert that year’s GDP; agreeing within ×/÷{mf:d1} is taken to mean they are in the same currency unit, not that they are the same rate (fiscal-year or multiple exchange rates make them differ). Differences of {threshold:pct1} or more are listed in the tooltip.
gold.note_fx_gap: The official rate is checked each year against the factor the World Bank used to convert that year’s GDP; agreeing within ×/÷{mf:d1} is taken to mean they are in the same currency unit, not that they are the same rate (fiscal-year or multiple exchange rates make them differ; in this chart for {year} they differ by up to {gap:pct1}). Differences of {threshold:pct1} or more are listed in the tooltip.
gold.note_median: The dots are medians from the same survey as the bar, drawn only where that survey also publishes a median.
gold.note_order: Which wage figure is used, by the same rule for every economy — coverage first, then the compilation that covers the most economies, so that as many economies as possible are compared on the same kind of figure: ILOSTAT average wages whose notes do not limit their coverage (where only monthly figures exist, converted with the same survey’s weekly hours) → OECD’s full-time-equivalent average wage (hourly via OECD’s usual weekly hours of full-time employees) → ILOSTAT average wages whose notes limit their coverage (e.g. urban only, private sector only, full-time only), marked “limited coverage”. Where an economy’s main figure differs from the previous year’s, the tooltip says so.
gold.note_sources: Each economy’s measure and the publisher’s notes are in the tooltip and the data table, and the figures used for it are in its profile. Gold: World Bank Pink Sheet monthly averages, averaged over the year; exchange rate: World Bank WDI annual average official rate.
gold.sub: Wage ÷ ({year} average gold price ÷ 31.1034768 g per troy ounce × that year’s average exchange rate). This is the same as converting the wage into US dollars at the market rate and dividing by the dollar price of a gram of gold.

how.note: “Healthy diet” is the World Bank Food Prices for Nutrition “cost of a healthy diet”: the cheapest locally available foods that together make up a healthy diet from six food groups, for one person for one day (priced in the International Comparison Program’s benchmark year; other years are the World Bank’s estimates from consumer price indices). “—” means the input could not be shown to be in the same currency unit as the World Bank’s local-currency series, or is missing (reasons under “Methods & sources”). International dollars: converted at the purchasing power parity of household consumption.
how.ruler_body: Local gold prices here are the US-dollar gold price × the exchange rate, so at any given time the ratio of two economies’ “grams of gold” equals the ratio of their wages converted at market exchange rates — gold does not remove the exchange rate. What changes the picture is step ②: the same gram of gold buys more where prices are lower. In step ③ the gold cancels out, so the result does not depend on measuring in gold at all.
how.step1_f_hour: = hourly wage ÷ local gold price per gram (US-dollar gold price × exchange rate)
how.step1_f_month: = monthly wage ÷ local gold price per gram (US-dollar gold price × exchange rate)
how.step2_f: = local gold price per gram ÷ cost of the cheapest healthy diet for one person for one day
how.step2_v: days of a healthy diet per gram
how.step3_f_hour: = hourly wage ÷ diet cost: the gold cancels out
how.step3_f_month: = monthly wage ÷ diet cost: the gold cancels out
how.step3_v_hour: days of a healthy diet per hour of work
how.step3_v_month: days of a healthy diet per month of work
how.sub_hour: One calculation for every economy: how many grams of gold an hour’s wage buys, then how much a gram of gold buys locally; multiplied together, that is what the hour of work buys.
how.sub_month: One calculation for every economy: how many grams of gold a month’s wage buys, then how much a gram of gold buys locally; multiplied together, that is what the month of work buys.

liv.mode_wage: As % of the {year} average monthly wage
liv.note_100: 100% means that what households consume in a month, per resident, equals one month of an employee’s average pay.
liv.note_fiscal: {list}: the World Bank keeps these economies’ national accounts by fiscal year, so consumption and the wage may cover different twelve months (the World Bank’s note is in the tooltip).
liv.note_gov: Services the government provides free or below cost (mainly health and education) are not counted; in ICP 2021 they range from {gmin:pct0} to {gmax:pct0} of household consumption across economies, so where they are paid for from taxes the ratio is lower, although the taxes come out of the mostly pre-tax wages.
liv.note_minority: {list}: fewer than half of the employed are employees, so the average wage describes a minority, and a short bar does not mean little pressure.
liv.note_not: It is not the share of anyone’s pay that their household spends: consumption is averaged over every resident, children included; households also live on other incomes (self-employment, pensions, benefits, property income), savings or borrowing; and consumption includes non-cash items such as an imputed rent for owner-occupied homes and food people grow themselves. It is not after tax: wages are employees’ averages, mostly before tax, and publishers often do not say which. It is not about low earners: both sides are averages.
liv.note_sensitivity: How a wage is measured moves this ratio as much as many real differences between economies: for the same economy and year, survey averages are ×{min:d2} to ×{max:d2} of OECD’s average wage (median ×{median:d2}, {n:int} cases), which moves the ratio the other way, ×{rlo:d2} to ×{rhi:d2}. Hollow dots show it with the other official average wages of the same year.
liv.note_switch: {list}: the wage source differs from the previous year; to compare years, use one continuous series (the chart over time below draws one for each focus economy).
liv.other_name: The same with another average wage of the same year

liv.sub: What households consume — food, rent (including an imputed rent for owner-occupied homes), energy, household goods, clothing, transport and all else, whether bought or produced for themselves — per resident per month, from the national accounts (World Bank), compared with employees’ average monthly wage for the same year (as each publisher dates its figures; where national accounts are kept by fiscal year, this is noted). Both are in local currency, so no exchange rate is needed. Services the government provides free (in many economies, much of health and education) are not in it. This is one angle on living pressure, not a subsistence line: both sides are averages.

liv.trend_note: Each line divides consumption per resident by the economy’s one continuous average-wage series (the same as in “Gold is a ruler that stretches”), year by year; this can be a different wage from the one in the ranking above, and the line breaks where the series breaks. Within one series, the change over time says more than levels across economies; it includes people consuming more as they get richer, not only prices.

liv.where_missing: {list}: no ICP composition of consumption (not published, or not passing the checks; see “Methods & sources”).
liv.where_no_wage: {list}: no verified average monthly wage for {year}; shown only as shares of consumption.
liv.where_none: No economy in view has an ICP composition of consumption.
liv.where_note: Rent is the housing that ICP leaves out of its “household consumption without housing”: rent paid by tenants and, for owners, an imputed rent, which statisticians estimate from the rents of similar homes or, in some economies, from costs such as depreciation and upkeep, which can be well below market rents. Mortgage payments are not counted as such: repaying the principal is a financial transaction and the interest is not consumption either; owners’ housing enters only as the imputed rent, so what owners with a mortgage pay each month is not shown here. Water, electricity, gas and other fuels are under “everything else”, as are toiletries and other personal-care goods, health, education and meals out. Purchases are generally counted where they are made, so visitors’ spending is inside the groups, and residents’ net spending abroad is shown apart where ICP publishes it. 2021 was a pandemic year in many economies.
liv.where_note_cons: Shares of household consumption, which need no wage; the number at the end is food, rent, household goods, clothing, transport and communication together. Sorted by the share of food for the home, which by Engel’s law tends to be lower where incomes are higher; as a share of national-accounts consumption it differs from survey-based Engel coefficients.
liv.where_note_wage: Each bar is the same ratio as above for {year}, divided into what the consumption consists of; the dashed line is one month’s average wage.
liv.where_sub: The World Bank’s International Comparison Program (ICP) publishes what consumption consists of only for its benchmark years, from the national accounts each economy supplies; this page reads the {years} benchmark, and other years’ composition is not estimated.
liv.where_title: Where the money goes: one resident’s monthly consumption ({year}, ICP benchmark year)
m.c_continuity: A change between two years of one source is compared with the change in nominal household consumption per head and in nominal GDP per head (World Bank local-currency values ÷ population); where it deviates from every available yardstick by more than OECD’s same-concept average wages have deviated from the same yardstick over as many years or fewer (against household consumption per head: {hfce}; against GDP per head: {gdp}), the notes say “the concept or scale may have changed” and the history lines break there; between two years whose notes on what the figure measures differ, or across a noted break, only a difference beyond ×/÷{tf:d2} is noted.
m.c_diet: The “cheapest healthy diet” covers food only, and takes the cheapest available foods, so it is not what a typical household actually spends; housing, health, education and social insurance — large items for living standards — are not in the food basket; ④ “Living costs and wages” counts all of household consumption, and “What costs more where” compares price levels by category.
m.c_excluded_notes: Records that ILOSTAT notes as “Value type: Real values” or marks with the observation status “Real value” (at some base year’s prices), records it notes as not an average or median wage (such as a minimum wage) or as in a time unit that does not match the indicator, and records with the observation status “Unreliable” or a low-reliability status are not used; other notes (such as remarks that a series “should be used with caution”) are shown verbatim.
m.c_extension: ILOSTAT republishes national surveys with a delay. For the publishers listed below, the survey publisher’s own release continues ILOSTAT’s series for the years after ILOSTAT’s latest, by the same rule for every economy: on every year both have, the publisher’s figures must agree with ILOSTAT’s within {tol:pct0}; the later years keep the series’ notes on what it measures (not ILOSTAT’s notes on its latest year alone, such as a break in series); and their currency unit is carried over only when the value moved by no more than ×/÷{mf:d1} from the latest earlier year of the series whose unit was established. Then they go through the same checks as any other figure. No other series is added: for every other economy, a series ends where ILOSTAT’s does. Publishers read so far: {list}.
m.c_ilostat: ILOSTAT compiles each economy’s official sources (labour force surveys, establishment surveys, administrative records), so concepts differ between economies. The publisher’s notes on each record (e.g. urban only, private sector only, net of tax, full-time only) are shown verbatim in tooltips and tables; records whose notes say they cover only part of the employees are labelled “limited coverage”, and a record without such notes is taken to cover all employees. A geographical note counts as limiting unless it states the whole national territory with no area excluded (overseas territories, which the World Bank lists as economies of their own, aside), and so does a maximum age; a minimum age does not (every survey counts employees from a working age). Order of preference, the same for every economy: ILOSTAT records whose notes do not limit their coverage → OECD → ILOSTAT records with limited coverage. A national statistical office’s own release is read only to continue a series ILOSTAT republishes, for the years ILOSTAT has not reached yet (see the next point).
m.c_intl_dollar: International dollars are the unit of the World Bank’s International Comparison Program: by construction, an international dollar buys in any economy what a US dollar buys in the United States. That is a convention of the unit, not a choice of this site.
m.c_living: Living costs (④): household final consumption of the national accounts (households and the non-profit institutions serving them) at purchasers’ prices, so taxes on products such as VAT are included, while income taxes, social contributions, buying homes, loan repayments and saving are not consumption; it includes an imputed rent for owner-occupied homes (estimated from the rents of similar homes or, in some economies, from costs) and food people grow themselves, and not the services the government provides free. It is used in a year only where it is shown to be in the wages’ currency unit, as exchange rates and PPPs are: it divides into the World Bank’s international-dollar figure as the PPP does, or it is carried over from an adjacent year by its own value or by its share of GDP (GDP being shown to be in that unit by the exchange rate), moving less than ×/÷{mf:d1}. Its composition comes only from the ICP benchmark (2021), where the parts must add up to ICP’s totals (actual individual consumption = household + government individual consumption), rent must lie between zero and ICP’s actual housing, and no remainder may be negative. Amounts (ICP’s shares × the World Bank’s current 2021 total) are shown only where the currency is known and the two totals are within ×/÷{mf:d1} in the same currency unit, judged by the ratios of the two publishers’ 2021 PPPs and dollar exchange rates; the tooltip gives how far apart they are. Residents per employed person (from the ILO’s modelled employment-to-population ratio and the World Bank’s population) and employees’ share of the employed (an ILO modelled estimate) are shown beside the ratio and never multiplied into it. Where the World Bank’s country notes say an economy’s national accounts are kept by fiscal year, the note is shown with its figures.
m.c_living_not: The consumption-to-wage ratio is not a composite pressure index: there are no weights, thresholds or colour bands. It compares two averages: per resident and per employee, mostly before tax, and it changes with how the wage is measured (the hollow dots and the sensitivity sentence show by how much), so differences between economies smaller than that are not a reliable ranking.
m.c_median: An average wage is usually higher than the median (a few high earners pull the average up). The dots are the median published by the same survey as the bar; where the bar comes from OECD, or the survey has no median, none is drawn, so that figures from different sources are not read as one distribution.
m.c_monthly_view: Each view uses, for every economy, the first figure in the order of preference that exists for that view, so an economy’s hourly and monthly views can use different figures (for example OECD’s monthly wage and an ILOSTAT survey’s hourly wage). Comparing monthly wages needs no assumption about hours. An hourly figure is published per hour by ILOSTAT, derived from an ILOSTAT monthly figure with the same survey’s hours, or OECD’s full-time-equivalent wage divided by OECD’s usual weekly hours of full-time employees; an economy with none of these appears only in the monthly view.
m.c_same_year: All economies use the same reference year’s wages, exchange rates, gold price and prices. The wage charts (①, ③ and ④) show only economies with a verified average wage for that year — except the food-group chart in ③ and the composition chart in ④, which use the benchmark year (the only year with these breakdowns) and that year’s wages, and ④’s chart over time, which follows each focus economy year by year; “Gold → goods” and the price-level chart also show economies without one. The top of the page lists the economies without a verified average wage for that year (with “{g20}”: the G20 member countries and the focus economies; with “{all}”: the focus economies).
m.c_time_units: Scale and time unit: one survey’s monthly and hourly figures, converted with that survey’s measured hours, should differ by no more than ×/÷{tf:d2} (the logarithmic midpoint of the week-to-month ratio {ug:d2}), and monthly ÷ hourly must lie between 1 and {hours:int} (the number of hours in a month); where the survey has no hours, they are converted with the median of other sources’ weekly hours that year (OECD’s usual hours of full-time employees included) and are judged wrong only from ×/÷{ug:d2}. The same kind of figure (mean or median) from different sources: within ×/÷{tf:d2} they confirm each other; at ×/÷{ug:d2} (a whole week-to-month factor) or more, one of them has a wrong unit or scale; in between, a difference of concept and a wrong time unit cannot be told apart, so the figures are kept and said to be unconfirmed. A month’s pay above a year’s GDP per head, or below a week’s household consumption per head, is taken as an unknown time unit or scale, and none of that survey’s figures in that time unit is used. Only another source can confirm a figure’s scale (one survey’s monthly and hourly figures come from the same data); when figures disagree and the data cannot tell which is wrong, none of them is used.
m.c_translation: The site’s text is available in the languages of the menu. English is the reference text; the other languages were translated from it with an AI model and reviewed in a second, independent pass — not by professional translators. Notes and survey names quoted from ILOSTAT stay in English, as ILOSTAT publishes them, and economies’ names come from your browser’s own list of names.
m.checks: Automatic checks (run on every refresh; if a check fails, no new data is published)
m.concepts: Differences in concept to keep in mind
m.excl_joins: Wages and diet costs are then joined to an exchange rate or PPP that passed these checks: an ILOSTAT wage ÷ the exchange rate (or ÷ the PPP) must match ILOSTAT’s own US-dollar (or PPP) value; the diet cost in local currency ÷ its PPP value must match the PPP; OECD’s constant-price national-currency wage ÷ its PPP-dollar value must match the PPP of the base year, or the currency OECD states must be the one the matching ILOSTAT records state.
m.excl_rates: Exchange rates and PPPs are checked only against the World Bank’s own data: the official rate against “GDP in local currency ÷ in US dollars”, the PPP against “household consumption in local currency ÷ in international dollars”, within ×/÷{mf:d1}; where the World Bank lacks these, the 2021 PPP is checked against the ICP 2021 price level of household consumption (relative to the United States, so it has no currency unit) × the official rate; a year with nothing to check carries over an adjacent year’s check (a value that moves by no more than ×/÷{mf:d1} is taken not to have changed unit); a year whose identity fails although its value moves by less than ×/÷{mf:d1} each year from a checked year is taken to be in the same unit — the inconsistency then has another, unknown cause — and is not used either.
m.excl_rule: Inputs that do not pass these checks are not used. The rules look only at the numbers and name no country, apart from the ICP’s base economy (the United States, whose price level defines the international dollar); each record’s kind, reason and numbers are below.
m.excl_units: Every number divides one institution’s figure (a wage) by another’s (an exchange rate, a PPP, a diet cost), so both must be in the same currency unit. Since 2000 (the first year of these data), the smallest factor of any non-par currency changeover has been the Irish pound’s (×{ie:d2}, in use alongside the euro’s fixed rate until 2002), followed by Latvia’s euro adoption in 2014 (×{lv:d2}). So two figures that differ by no more than ×/÷{mf:d1} are taken to be in the same unit — though not to be the same number: from 2002 on, a change of unit would move them apart by at least ×{lv:d2}, unless they also differ for another reason in the opposite direction, which this check cannot rule out. For 2000–2001 the bound cannot tell Irish pounds from euros; Ireland’s figures for those years here are OECD’s, stated in euros.
m.f_gold: Local gold price (local currency per gram) = the year’s average gold price (US$ per troy ounce) ÷ 31.1034768 × the year’s average exchange rate (local currency per US$)
m.f_ilo: An ILOSTAT monthly figure whose survey has no usable hourly wage: hourly wage = monthly wage ÷ (that survey’s weekly hours actually worked × 52 ÷ 12); without such hours it has no hourly figure and can be compared only in the monthly view
m.f_living: ④ One resident’s monthly consumption as % of the wage = household final consumption (World Bank, local currency) ÷ population ÷ 12 ÷ the average monthly wage for the same year; its composition = ICP 2021 expenditure on each group ÷ ICP 2021 household consumption (rent = household consumption − household consumption without housing), applied to the World Bank’s 2021 total
m.f_oecd: OECD data: hourly wage = full-time-equivalent average annual wage ÷ (usual weekly hours of full-time employees × 52)
m.f_step1: ① Gold per hour of work (g) = hourly wage (local currency) ÷ local gold price
m.f_step2_diet: ② Days of healthy diet per gram of gold = local gold price ÷ cost of the cheapest healthy diet for one person for one day (local currency)
m.f_step2_intl: ② Purchasing power of 1 g of gold (international $) = US-dollar gold price per gram ÷ price level of household consumption (PPP ÷ exchange rate)
m.f_step3: ③ Hourly wage at PPP = hourly wage ÷ household-consumption PPP = ① × ② (the pipeline recomputes this for every record as an arithmetic self-test)
m.src_note: Snapshot = the raw bytes the publisher returned, unmodified; the SHA-256 lets you verify a file has not been altered. Refresh: daily at 07:23 UTC and whenever the pipeline code changes; it can also be run from the repository’s Actions page (“data-refresh” → “Run workflow”). This table lists the files read to build this dataset; earlier versions of each file remain in the repository’s history for audit. Raw-file links point to the branch the site was built from ({branch}).
m.sub: Every number can be traced to a file an official publisher released. The pipeline code, the raw snapshots and the check results are all in the repository.

ps.note_cols: Columns: Consumption = household consumption, i.e. the final consumption of households and non-profit institutions serving households as a whole; Food = food and non-alcoholic beverages; Housing = housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels. The Housing, Health and Education columns use ICP’s “actual individual consumption” concept, which includes what governments and non-profit institutions provide to households, not only what households pay themselves.
ps.note_year: This chart uses ICP 2021 as published; the yearly overall price level used in the other sections comes from World Bank WDI, and the two can differ slightly for 2021 because of revisions. Prices and exchange rates have changed since 2021, so this is not a precise picture of today’s gaps (for the yearly overall level see “② Gold → goods”, in international dollars).
ps.spread#one: Across the {n:int} economy in ICP 2021 that is on the World Bank’s list of economies, the middle half of food and non-alcoholic beverage price levels spans a factor of ×{food:d2} (75th ÷ 25th percentile); for services: {services}.
ps.spread#other: Across the {n:int} economies in ICP 2021 that are on the World Bank’s list of economies, the middle half of food and non-alcoholic beverage price levels spans a factor of ×{food:d2} (75th ÷ 25th percentile); for services: {services}.
ps.spread_conclusion: Goods that can be traded across borders, like food, are priced more alike across economies than local services.

real.note: Log scale. US dollars at the market rate = grams of gold × the dollar price of a gram, because every local gold price is the dollar price × the exchange rate. The international dollar has the purchasing power of a US dollar in the United States (the ICP convention), so for the United States the two values coincide.
real.sub_hour: For each economy, the same hourly wage converted two ways: at the market exchange rate into US dollars (grey — the same as measuring in grams of gold) and at purchasing power parity into international dollars (blue — local prices taken into account). The distance between the two dots is how much local prices narrow or widen the gap.
real.sub_month: For each economy, the same monthly wage converted two ways: at the market exchange rate into US dollars (grey — the same as measuring in grams of gold) and at purchasing power parity into international dollars (blue — local prices taken into account). ruler.callout_down: From {y0} to {y1} the annual average gold price fell from US${a0:int} to US${a1:int} per troy ounce. A wage measured in grams of gold rises whenever gold falls or rises more slowly than the wage, even if what the wage buys locally has not changed.
ruler.callout_up: From {y0} to {y1} the annual average gold price rose from US${a0:int} to US${a1:int} per troy ounce (×{r:d1}). A wage measured in grams of gold falls whenever gold rises faster than the wage, even if what the wage buys locally has not changed.
ruler.gold_note: World Bank Pink Sheet monthly averages (per the workbook’s description, averages of daily spot prices since June 2025, of London afternoon fixings before). The benchmark price is published in US dollars.
ruler.gold_title: Gold price, US$ per troy ounce (monthly average, log scale)
ruler.hist_breaks: Lines are broken, so that two figures that may not be comparable are not joined, where: the publisher notes a break in series or a change of coverage (such as ILOSTAT’s “Break in series”); ILOSTAT’s notes on what the figure measures change; or the change between two points of one source, compared with the change in nominal household consumption and GDP per head over the same years (World Bank local-currency values ÷ population), is out of line with every available one of them by more than OECD’s same-concept average wages have been over as many years or fewer (against household consumption per head: {bounds}), or cannot be checked.
ruler.hist_note: Each year’s monthly wage is converted with that year’s average gold price and average exchange rate.
ruler.hist_rule#one: One series per economy, by the same rule for every economy: among OECD’s full-time-equivalent wage and each ILOSTAT survey’s average monthly wage with at least {n:int} year, the one with the most years not restricted in coverage.
ruler.hist_rule#other: One series per economy, by the same rule for every economy: among OECD’s full-time-equivalent wage and each ILOSTAT survey’s average monthly wage with at least {n:int} years, the one with the most years not restricted in coverage.
ruler.hist_title: Average monthly wage in grams of gold (annual, log scale)
ruler.isolated: Isolated points (broken on both sides) are drawn as dots.
ruler.local_none: There is no year in which all focus economies have a verified exchange rate.
ruler.local_note: Annual average gold price × annual average official exchange rate, as an index with {year} = 100 (the first year in which every focus economy has one).
